questions.q: A dermatologist biopsies a lesion from a child with classic Pityriasis Lichenoides Chronica. Which histopathological finding would most reliably distinguish this condition from Pityriasis Lichenoides et Varioliformis Acuta (PLEVA)?
opts: Presence of dense dermal fibrosis with extensive scar formation
Marked epidermal necrosis with massive extravasation of erythrocytes and severe basal vacuolization
Mild superficial perivascular infiltrate with focal compact parakeratosis, pseudo-Munro abscesses, and minimal epidermal necrosis
Complete absence of interface dermatitis and normal stratum corneum architecture
questions.exp: Classic PLC histology is noticeably milder than PLEVA, featuring a superficial perivascular lymphohistiocytic infiltrate, vacuolar interface dermatitis, focal compact parakeratosis, and exocytosis forming pseudo-Munro abscesses, with minimal to absent epidermal necrosis and erythrocyte extravasation. PLEVA, by contrast, shows severe epidermal necrosis, marked erythrocyte extravasation, and severe basal vacuolization. The absence of varioliform scarring clinically in PLC also distinguishes it from PLEVA.

questions.q: Histopathological examination of a slowly progressive dermal nodule on the elbow of a 6-year-old child shows nodules of spindle-shaped endothelial cells arranged in a 'tufted' pattern within the mid to deep dermis. The lesion is clinically confined to the dermis and upper subcutis with hypertrichosis overlying the site. Under the ISSVA classification, what is the most likely diagnosis?
opts: Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma with benign course
Tufted angioma representing the superficial, mild end of the KHE spectrum
GLUT1-positive infantile haemangioma with dermal involution
Pyogenic granuloma with secondary follicular hyperplasia
questions.exp: Tufted angioma (also known as angioblastoma of Nakagawa) is histologically characterised by nodules of spindle-shaped endothelial cells and is classified by ISSVA as a benign vascular tumour, yet it exists on the same biological spectrum as kaposiform haemangioendothelioma—representing the superficial, indolent end. The confinement to dermis and slow lateral extension before stabilisation, along with the characteristic tufted histology, are diagnostic features distinguishing TA from the deeper, locally aggressive KHE.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 3] Kaposiform Haemangioendothelioma and Tufted Angioma

questions.q: A 3-month-old infant with aplasia cutis congenita shows healing with dermal scarring devoid of hair follicles and eccrine glands. Which genetic pathway is NOT implicated in the pathogenesis of this condition?
opts: Ribosome biogenesis defects (BMS1 mutations in Group 1)
Rho GTPase signaling abnormalities (ARHGAP31 mutations in Adams-Oliver syndrome)
HLA-mediated autoimmune destruction of keratinocytes
Notch signaling disruption (NOTCH1/DLL4 mutations in Group 2)
questions.exp: Aplasia cutis congenita is explicitly a structural anomaly caused by genetic mutations, teratogens, vascular events, or intrauterine trauma—NOT an autoimmune, immunobullous, or antibody-mediated disease. Therefore, HLA-mediated autoimmune destruction plays no role in ACC pathogenesis, and there are no known HLA associations with this condition. The other options (BMS1, ARHGAP31, Notch pathway) are documented genetic mechanisms in various ACC groups.

questions.q: A 4-year-old presents with rubella infection. On intraoral examination, you note pinpoint rose-pink macules on the soft palate and uvula. What is the eponymous name for this characteristic enanthem?
opts: Koplik spots
Forchheimer spots
Roseola spots
Scarlatinal spots
questions.exp: Forchheimer spots are the pathognomonic enanthem of rubella, consisting of pinpoint rose-pink macules or petechiae on the soft palate and uvula, appearing just prior to or alongside the cutaneous rash. This finding helps clinically distinguish rubella from other viral exanthems, as Koplik spots are specific to measles.

questions.q: A mother presents at term with primary genital HSV infection. What is the approximate risk of vertical transmission to the neonate?
opts: Less than 1–3%
questions.exp: Primary maternal genital HSV infection near delivery in the third trimester carries a catastrophic 30–50% transmission risk due to high viral shedding and absent protective transplacental maternal antibodies. This contrasts sharply with recurrent maternal infection, which carries <1–3% risk. Notably, 70–90% of infected neonates are born to asymptomatic mothers with no known herpes history.

questions.q: A 3-month-old infant presents with a rapidly enlarging, poorly demarcated violaceous plaque on the neck extending into the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue. Laboratory studies reveal thrombocytopenia (45,000/μL), elevated D-dimer, and prolonged PT/INR. Which of the following best explains the pathophysiology of the coagulopathy in this case?
opts: GLUT1-positive infantile haemangioma triggering consumption of platelets through shear stress
Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma causing consumptive coagulopathy via the Kasabach-Merritt Phenomenon
Congenital RICH with intralesional thrombosis activating the extrinsic pathway
Pyogenic granuloma with bacterial superinfection producing endotoxin-mediated coagulopathy
questions.exp: Kaposiform haemangioendothelioma (KHE) and tufted angioma are unique among vascular tumours in their capacity to trigger the life-threatening Kasabach-Merritt Phenomenon—a consumptive coagulopathy characterised by thrombocytopenia and hypofibrinaemia due to sequestration and consumption of platelets and coagulation factors within the tumour. This shared biological property is the key feature distinguishing KHE/TA from the much commoner GLUT1-positive infantile haemangioma, which does NOT cause KMP.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 3] Kaposiform Haemangioendothelioma and Tufted Angioma

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate presents with a round, punched-out defect on the scalp vertex covered by a thin, translucent epithelial membrane. On examination, there is a ring of dark, coarse, radially oriented hair surrounding the lesion. What is the pathological significance of this hair collar sign?
opts: It indicates an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern requiring genetic counseling
It is a pathognomonic clinical marker for an underlying neural tube defect and warrants neuroimaging
It confirms the diagnosis of Adams-Oliver syndrome with limb involvement
It demonstrates active inflammation and predicts poor wound healing outcomes
questions.exp: The hair collar sign—a ring of dark, coarse, radially oriented hair surrounding membranous aplasia cutis congenita—is a pathognomonic clinical marker that indicates an underlying neural tube defect. This finding necessitates imaging evaluation (ultrasound or MRI) to assess for associated CNS anomalies. The hair collar does not indicate inheritance pattern or guarantee other syndromic features.

questions.q: Pigmentary mosaicism represents a genetically determined embryological anomaly. Which of the following statements regarding the genetics and pathogenesis of these conditions is CORRECT?
opts: Caused by autosomal dominant inherited mutations with variable penetrance and expressivity
Pathogenesis involves specific pathogenic antibody isotypes, HLA associations, and inflammatory cytokine cascades
Results from postzygotic somatic mutations occurring early in embryogenesis and is therefore strictly sporadic
Over 90% of cases show mutations in genes unrelated to pigmentation pathways
questions.exp: Pigmentary mosaicism is caused by postzygotic somatic chromosomal alterations (mutations, aneuploidies, or translocations) occurring early in embryogenesis, making these conditions strictly sporadic and not inherited. Over 90% of chromosomal aberrations overlap with known pigmentation genes. These are not autoimmune or inflammatory diseases—they lack pathogenic antibodies, autoantigens, inflammatory cascades, and HLA associations.

questions.q: A 2-year-old boy presents with multiple reddish-brown macules and papules on his trunk and thighs. On stroking one lesion, immediate localized erythema and whealing develop. Histopathology reveals a 40-fold increase in mast cells predominantly in the papillary dermis. Which genetic mutation is MOST likely to be absent in this child's clonal mast cells?
opts: KIT D816V mutation in exon 17
KIT mutation in the transmembrane domain (exons 8–11)
TET2 mutation
Germline KIT mutation outside exon 17
questions.exp: In pediatric mastocytosis, only 42% carry the D816V mutation; up to 44% have mutations outside exon 17 in extracellular/transmembrane domains. Germline KIT mutations are associated with familial cases (2–4% overall), making them rare in sporadic childhood cutaneous mastocytosis. The strong positive Darier's sign and papillary dermis location confirm maculopapular cutaneous mastocytosis (urticaria pigmentosa).

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy with loose anagen syndrome presents with focal patches of matted, unruly hair primarily on the occipital scalp that worsen after sleeping. No other systemic features are noted. Which histopathological layer is the site of the primary structural defect in this condition?
opts: Defective keratinization of the medulla of the hair shaft
Faulty keratinization of the inner root sheath (IRS) with impaired adhesion to the hair cuticle
Inflammatory infiltration of the dermal papilla and bulb
Premature entry into catagen phase due to follicular stem cell exhaustion
questions.exp: Loose anagen syndrome is characterized by a structural defect strictly localized to the inner root sheath (IRS) of anagen hair follicles. Faulty or premature keratinization of the IRS leads to profoundly impaired adhesion between the cuticle of the hair shaft and the companion layer of the IRS. This mechanical defect—not inflammatory or immune-mediated—allows minor friction to easily dislodge the poorly anchored anagen hairs.

questions.q: A 45-year-old woman presents with discrete telangiectatic macules on a tan background with minimal hyperpigmentation and an absent Darier's sign. Skin biopsy confirms mastocytosis. Which histopathological finding distinguishes the underlying pathogenesis of her disease from a typical autoimmune blistering disorder?
opts: Presence of CD25+ and CD2+ aberrant mast cells (absent on normal reactive mast cells)
Detection of circulating IgG autoantibodies against desmosomal proteins
Granule deposition along the basement membrane zone
HLA-B27 association with disease susceptibility
questions.exp: Mastocytosis is a neoplastic myeloproliferative disorder driven by somatic KIT mutations, not autoimmunity. The defining feature is clonal expansion of mast cells aberrantly expressing CD25 and/or CD2 surface markers—receptors strictly absent on normal reactive mast cells. This distinguishes it from autoimmune diseases, which lack target autoantigens, autoantibodies, or HLA associations. Her telangiectatic macules describe TMEP (Telangiectasia Macularis Eruptiva Perstans), the adult variant.

questions.q: A neonate presents at birth with generalized dark blue, non-blanching macules and papules across the trunk and extremities. Histopathology shows poorly circumscribed aggregates of nucleated erythroid precursor cells, immature leukocytes, and megakaryocytes within the dermis. Which pathophysiological mechanism best explains this clinical presentation?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of dermal melanocytes leading to pigmentation loss
Cutaneous extramedullary hematopoiesis as a response to profound fetal systemic stress
Primary vasculitis of the superficial and reticular dermal vessels
Abnormal migration of neural crest-derived cells during embryogenesis
questions.exp: The 'blueberry muffin baby' represents a morphological reaction pattern of cutaneous extramedullary hematopoiesis (EMH), not autoimmunity or vasculitis. In response to overwhelming fetal stress (infection, severe anemia, or bone marrow replacement), the dermal mesenchyme reverts to its embryonic hematopoietic function. Histopathology characteristically shows nucleated blood cell precursors without true inflammation or vasculitis.

questions.q: A 3-week-old infant presents with asymptomatic streaky brown macules following the lines of Blaschko on the trunk and extremities. Histology shows increased melanin in basal keratinocytes with normal melanocyte count and no dermal melanophages. Which diagnosis best fits this clinical and histopathological presentation?
opts: Hypomelanosis of Ito with dermal involvement
Linear and Whorled Nevoid Hypermelanosis (LWNH)
Segmental neurofibromatosis type 1
Inflammatory linear verrucous epidermal nevus (ILVEN)
questions.exp: LWNH classically presents in the first few weeks of life with diffuse, asymptomatic streaky hyperpigmented macules following Blaschko lines, lacking any preceding vesicular or inflammatory stage. The histology is pathognomonic: epidermal melanotic hypermelanosis with increased melanin in basal keratinocytes, normal melanocyte number, and crucially—no dermal melanophages or pigment incontinence, distinguishing it from other pigmentary disorders.

questions.q: A 6-year-old boy presents with ivory-white papules and nodules on his back that coalesce into a reticular 'pebbly' pattern. He also has extensive dermal melanocytosis and generalized hirsutism, but notably clear corneas on slit-lamp examination. His mother is an asymptomatic carrier. Which enzymatic deficiency is responsible for this clinical presentation?
opts: Alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency
Iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency
Hexosaminidase A deficiency
Glucocerebrosidase deficiency
questions.exp: The pathognomonic ivory-white papules coalescing into a 'pebbly' pattern on the back, combined with X-linked inheritance (carrier mother) and absent corneal clouding, is diagnostic of Hunter Syndrome (MPS II), caused by iduronate-2-sulfatase deficiency. MPS I (Hurler Syndrome) presents with similar hirsutism and melanocytosis but includes severe corneal clouding, distinguishing it from this case.

questions.q: A 3-year-old boy presents with severe blistering sunburns after minimal sun exposure, progressive neurological decline, short stature, and gonadal hypoplasia. Genetic testing confirms mutations in the XPA gene. Which of the following best describes the PRIMARY cellular defect in this patient's condition?
opts: Failure of translesion DNA synthesis polymerase
Inability to verify and recognize UV-induced DNA photoproducts in the nucleotide excision repair pathway
Defective helicase activity within the TFIIH transcription-repair complex
Loss of autoimmune regulation with pathogenic anti-basement membrane antibodies
questions.exp: XP-A results from mutations in the XPA gene encoding the XPA protein responsible for DNA damage verification in nucleotide excision repair. The patient's severe neurological involvement and the clinical tetrad (severe XP, mental deficiency, dwarfism, gonadal hypoplasia) indicate De Sanctis-Cacchione Syndrome, the most severe XP-A phenotype. Xeroderma pigmentosum is fundamentally a DNA repair disorder, NOT an autoimmune or immunobullous disease.

questions.q: A 5-day-old premature infant born at 28 weeks gestation with sepsis presents with rapidly progressive, board-like induration of the skin starting on the buttocks and thighs, with characteristic sparing of the palms and soles. Histology shows fat necrosis with doubly refractile, needle-shaped clefts arranged radially within adipocytes and absent inflammation. What is the primary pathophysiological mechanism underlying this presentation?
opts: Autoimmune destruction of subcutaneous adipose tissue via IgG autoantibodies against lipid antigens
Crystallization and solidification of neonatal fat due to high saturated fatty acid content combined with peripheral circulatory collapse and immature lipolytic mechanisms
Vasculitis-mediated inflammation of the subcutaneous vasculature causing secondary fat necrosis
Bacterial lipase production by septic organisms directly hydrolyzing subcutaneous triglycerides
questions.exp: Sclerema neonatorum results from the unique biochemistry of neonatal fat, which has a very high ratio of saturated fatty acids (palmitic and stearic acids) to unsaturated fatty acids, giving it a higher melting point. In severely ill premature infants, peripheral circulatory collapse causes skin cooling; the immature enzymatic lipolytic mechanisms cannot mobilize fat for heat generation, leading to rapid crystallization of subcutaneous fat. The histological finding of doubly refractile needle-shaped clefts represents dissolved triglyceride crystals, confirming the crystallization mechanism rather than inflammatory or immunological pathogenesis.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 4] Sclerema neonatorum vs Subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn

questions.q: A histopathology specimen from a critically ill neonate with sclerema neonatorum is examined under polarized light microscopy. Which of the following histological findings is considered pathognomonic for this condition?
opts: Dense lymphocytic infiltration in the subcutaneous septa with neutrophilic microabscesses
Vasculitis with fibrinoid necrosis of dermal and subcutaneous blood vessels
Doubly refractile, needle-shaped clefts arranged radially within adipocytes with striking absence of inflammation
Granulomatous inflammation with giant cells surrounding areas of fat necrosis
questions.exp: The pathognomonic histological hallmark of sclerema neonatorum is the presence of doubly refractile, needle-shaped clefts arranged radially within adipocytes, which represent dissolved triglyceride crystals. Critically, there is a striking absence of inflammatory infiltrate or very sparse inflammation, distinguishing it from other forms of panniculitis. The thickened connective tissue septa reflect massive edema rather than inflammatory cell infiltration.
questions.source: [Paeds Day 4] Sclerema neonatorum vs Subcutaneous fat necrosis of newborn

questions.q: A 6-month-old boy presents with recurrent unexplained fever episodes and poor thermoregulation. On examination, he has sparse, lightly pigmented scalp hair, frontal bossing, a depressed nasal bridge, and periorbital hyperpigmentation. Intraoral examination reveals conical-shaped upper central incisors. A skin biopsy from the palm shows total absence of eccrine sweat glands and ducts. Which gene mutation is most likely responsible for this presentation?
opts: Mutations in the EDA1 gene on chromosome Xq12-q13.1
Mutations in the EDAR gene on chromosome 2q11-q13
Mutations in the EDARADD gene on chromosome 1q42.2-q43
Autosomal dominant mutations affecting TP53 signaling
questions.exp: This is a classic presentation of X-linked Hypohidrotic Ectodermal Dysplasia (XLHED) or Christ-Siemens-Touraine Syndrome, which accounts for ~80% of HED cases. The triad of severe hypohidrosis, hypotrichosis, and hypodontia with conical incisors, combined with the characteristic facies and skin biopsy findings, confirms XLHED caused by EDA1 gene mutations encoding Ectodysplasin-A ligand. The male infant presentation indicates X-linked recessive inheritance.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with multiple dome-shaped, flesh-colored papules on his hands with a rough surface and pathognomonic black dots. Histological examination reveals hyperkeratosis, acanthosis, papillomatosis forming 'church spires', and koilocytes in the upper stratum spinosum. Which HPV type is most likely responsible?
opts: HPV-3
HPV-1
HPV-10
HPV-28
questions.exp: Common warts (verruca vulgaris) are caused by HPV 1, 2, 4, 27, and 57. The clinical and histological features described—exophytic dome-shaped papules, punctate black dots representing thrombosed capillary loops, and the pathognomonic 'church spires' with koilocytes—are diagnostic of common warts. HPV-3, HPV-10, and HPV-28 cause flat warts, which present as small, flat-topped papules lacking papillomatosis.

questions.q: A previously vaccinated 8-year-old develops an unusual measles presentation with prominent pulmonary infiltrates, petechiae, purpura, and peripheral edema alongside the rash. Which variant of measles does this clinical picture most likely represent?
opts: Classic (ordinary) measles with superimposed pneumonia
Atypical measles occurring in a host with altered or partial immunity
Measles complicated by secondary bacterial infection
Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis in early stages
questions.exp: Atypical measles is a severe variant that occurs in individuals with partial or altered immunity, typically from previous vaccination. This form is distinguished by pronounced pulmonary involvement with prominent infiltrates and pneumonitis, along with severe cutaneous manifestations including petechiae, purpura, and significant edema—findings that differentiate it from the classic maculopapular blanching rash of ordinary measles.

questions.q: A mother brings her 4-year-old daughter to clinic reporting patchy areas where her daughter does not sweat, alternating with normal sweating regions in a striped pattern along the trunk and limbs. The girl has whorled areas of sparse hair, conical upper incisors, and characteristic facial features. Genetic testing confirms a heterozygous EDA1 gene mutation. Which mechanism explains the clinical presentation of variable features in this female carrier?
opts: Random X-chromosome inactivation (Lyonization) creating cellular mosaicism
Incomplete penetrance of an autosomal dominant mutation
Skewed autosomal gene dosage compensation
Mitochondrial heteroplasmy affecting sweat gland development
questions.exp: Female carriers of X-linked Hypohidrotic Ectodermal Dysplasia demonstrate variable, milder features due to random X-chromosome inactivation (Lyonization). This process silences one X chromosome randomly in each cell during early development, creating cellular mosaicism. The alternating bands of normal and absent sweating along Blaschko's lines, combined with whorled patches of sparse hair, are pathognomonic signs of this X-chromosome inactivation pattern in heterozygous females.

questions.q: A 7-year-old boy presents with a 4-month history of small, red-brown papules on his trunk and proximal arms. The lesions are asymptomatic and have a characteristic tightly adherent scale that, when scraped away, reveals a shining brown surface underneath. Which immunological cell type predominantly mediates the pathogenesis of this condition?
opts: CD8+ cytotoxic T-cells with autoantibodies against dermal keratinocytes
CD4+ helper T-cells with some expressing FoxP3, triggered by exogenous antigens
B-cells producing IgG autoantibodies against the basement membrane zone
Neutrophils and complement-mediated immune complexes
questions.exp: Pityriasis Lichenoides Chronica is driven by a T-cell-mediated cellular immune response, predominantly CD4+ helper T-cells (unlike PLEVA which is CD8-mediated), with some T-cells expressing FoxP3 suggesting a regulatory phenotype accounting for the chronic nature. The disease is triggered by exogenous antigens such as infectious agents and is NOT autoantibody-mediated. CD8+ predominance, autoantibodies, and immune complex mechanisms characterize other conditions but not PLC.

questions.q: A 2-day-old neonate born to a mother with documented rubella infection during the first trimester presents with blueberry muffin lesions. Which additional clinical triad is classically associated with congenital rubella and helps distinguish it from other TORCH-related causes of EMH?
opts: Periventricular intracranial calcifications, sensorineural deafness, and hepatosplenomegaly
Congenital cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart defects (patent ductus arteriosus)
Diffuse tram-track intracerebral calcifications, chorioretinitis, and hydrocephalus
Microcephaly, periosteal reactions, and persistent ductus venosus
questions.exp: Rubella is the classic historical prototype for the blueberry muffin baby and is characterized by the triad of congenital cataracts, sensorineural deafness, and congenital heart defects (classically patent ductus arteriosus). CMV causes periventricular calcifications, while toxoplasmosis causes diffuse/tram-track calcifications—these distinguishing features aid in differential diagnosis of congenital infections presenting with EMH.

questions.q: A 5-year-old child presents with a 3-day history of high fever, coryza, conjunctivitis, and barking cough. On examination, you observe small bright red macules with blue-white centers on the buccal mucosa opposite the premolar teeth. What is the clinical significance of these oral findings?
opts: They represent secondary bacterial infection requiring immediate antibiotic therapy
They are pathognomonic for measles and appear 48 hours prior to the characteristic exanthem
They indicate severe vitamin A deficiency and portend poor prognosis
They are viral vesicles that will rupture and form crusts
questions.exp: Koplik's spots are the pathognomonic enanthem of measles, appearing as tiny bright red macules with blue-white ('grains of sand') centers on the buccal mucosa. These lesions characteristically erupt 48 hours before the appearance of the exanthem, making them crucial early diagnostic markers. Their presence during the prodromal phase helps confirm measles diagnosis before the rash develops.

questions.q: A 3-year-old child with autosomal recessive inheritance presents with coarse facial features ('gargoylism'), severe generalized hypertrichosis, and extensive Mongolian blue spots. Slit-lamp examination reveals bilateral corneal clouding. Histopathology shows characteristic 'gargoyle cells' in the sweat glands with metachromatic material in the dermis. Which gene mutation is most likely responsible?
opts: IDS gene (Hunter Syndrome)
IDUA gene (Hurler Syndrome)
GLA gene (Fabry Disease)
SGSH gene (Sanfilippo Syndrome)
questions.exp: The combination of autosomal recessive inheritance, severe gargoylism, generalized hypertrichosis, extensive dermal melanocytosis, and crucially, bilateral corneal clouding, is pathognomonic for Hurler Syndrome (MPS I severe variant), caused by alpha-L-iduronidase deficiency from IDUA gene mutations. The absence of the pebbly ivory papules and X-linked pattern excludes Hunter Syndrome.

questions.q: A 4-year-old girl presents with diffusely sparse, dull, and unruly hair that has never grown long. Her parents report that she rarely needs haircuts. Dermoscopy shows easily pluckable anagen hairs with poor anchorage to the follicle. Which genetic defect is most commonly associated with this clinical presentation?
opts: Heterozygous missense mutation (E337K) in the K6HF keratin gene (KRT75)
Homozygous loss-of-function mutation in the POFUT2 gene
Heterozygous mutation in the SHOC2 gene on chromosome 10q25
X-linked recessive mutation in the AR gene affecting androgen receptor function
questions.exp: Loose anagen syndrome Type A (classic/unruly type) is most commonly caused by a heterozygous missense mutation (E337K) in the K6HF keratin gene (KRT75), which disrupts normal keratinization of the inner root sheath. This defect leads to impaired adhesion between the hair shaft cuticle and the IRS companion layer, resulting in mechanical hair shedding despite normal hair growth phase entry. The SHOC2 mutation is associated specifically with syndromic LAS presenting with Noonan-like features.

questions.q: A 6-year-old child presents with a 3-day history of a light pink macular rash that started on the face and spread downward to the trunk and extremities. Examination reveals tender suboccipital and postauricular lymphadenopathy that preceded the rash by 5 days. Which viral family does the causative agent of rubella belong to?
opts: Paramyxoviridae
Togaviridae
Picornaviridae
Coronaviridae
questions.exp: Rubella virus is an enveloped, single-stranded RNA virus belonging to the genus Rubivirus within the Togaviridae family. The characteristic early lymphadenopathy preceding the faint, rapidly fading rash helps distinguish rubella from measles, which causes a more confluent exanthem.

questions.q: A neonate born via vaginal delivery presents on day 10 of life with grouped vesicles on an erythematous base over the left scalp and cheek, along with keratoconjunctivitis. Examination shows no hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, or signs of encephalitis. Which clinical classification best fits this presentation?
opts: Congenital intrauterine HSV infection
Skin-Eye-Mouth (SEM) disease
Disseminated neonatal HSV
Neonatal HSV encephalitis
questions.exp: This presentation exemplifies SEM disease: onset at day 10 (typical days 9–11), grouped vesicles on erythematous base at the presenting fetal part (scalp/cheek from delivery trauma), keratoconjunctivitis, and critically—absence of visceral organ involvement or CNS signs. SEM disease has 0% mortality if recognized and treated promptly, though ~90% will have cutaneous recurrences.

questions.q: A 10-year-old girl with plantar warts notices that her lesions differ from the calluses on her heels. The key distinguishing clinical feature of plantar warts from calluses is:
opts: Presence of hyperkeratosis on histology
Interruption of natural dermatoglyphic skin lines
Endophytic growth pattern
Location on weight-bearing areas
questions.exp: Plantar warts are thick, painful, endophytic hyperkeratotic papules on weight-bearing areas. The critical bedside distinguishing feature from calluses is that plantar warts interrupt the natural dermatoglyphic (fingerprint-like) skin lines of the plantar surface, whereas calluses preserve these lines. This clinical finding allows rapid differentiation without histology.

questions.q: Which of the following epidemiological statements regarding xeroderma pigmentosum is CORRECT?
opts: XP is an autosomal dominant condition with male predominance affecting primarily individuals of African descent
The incidence in Japan (1 in 20,000 to 1 in 80,000) is significantly higher than in the USA (1 in 250,000), primarily due to a founder mutation in the XPA gene
Skin manifestations typically begin within the first few days of life at birth
XP-A accounts for only 5–10% of cases worldwide but represents 90% of cases in Japan
questions.exp: Xeroderma pigmentosum is an autosomal recessive disorder with equal sex incidence occurring in all ethnic groups. The incidence is dramatically higher in Japan (1 in 20,000–80,000) compared to the USA (1 in 250,000) and Western Europe (2.3 per million), a difference attributable to a founder mutation in the XPA gene that is prevalent in the Japanese population. The median age of symptom onset is 1–2 years, NOT at birth.
